name: repository
intent: Mediates between the domain model and the data mapping layer with a collection-like interface, so domain code adds, removes and finds persistent objects as if they lived in memory and never constructs queries or touches persistence APIs itself.
problem: Persistence code spreads: every application service re-derives the same SQL or ORM queries, duplicate query logic drifts apart, table and column names leak into domain decisions, and testing domain rules without a database becomes impossible. Callers should be able to think in collections of domain objects instead of queries.
context: Applies to systems with a non-trivial domain model sitting on a data-mapping layer (Data Mapper, metadata mapping, or a hand-written mapper) where the same queries recur across application services; it becomes more valuable as domain classes and query volume grow. It is the standard persistence boundary of DDD aggregates (one repository per aggregate root) and presumes a unit of work or session that owns flush and commit. It is not a per-table data-access wrapper and not a replacement for transaction control.
benefits: Query construction is concentrated in one place per aggregate, so duplicate query logic disappears and a query change is a one-site change.
The domain reads like collection operations (add, remove, find by identity, find by domain criterion), which keeps business rules free of SQL, table names and ORM session calls.
Testability: an in-memory implementation of the same interface lets domain logic be unit-tested without a database, and it is the seam the framework guidance explicitly recommends.
One-way dependency: the domain defines the interface and the infrastructure implements it, so the store can be replaced, replicated or split off without touching domain code.

Fetch strategy (eager/lazy, projections, caching, logging, authorization) can be attached centrally — including through decorators around the interface — instead of being re-decided at every call site.
Domain-language method names (findOverdueInvoices) make the queries part of the ubiquitous language and reviewable by domain experts.
tradeoffs: The collection abstraction leaks: complex or aggregate-specific queries either grow the interface until it becomes a query builder, or callers bypass the repository and the abstraction is dead weight.

Redundancy when the persistence framework already implements Repository: EF Core DbContext, Spring Data interfaces, TypeORM Repository<T> and ActiveRecord relations are repository surfaces, so a one-to-one wrapper duplicates an API and hides the framework's powers (the documented criticism of repositories over ORMs).

Performance is hidden: collection-looking calls still execute SQL, so per-object fetches, N+1 loading and eager joins become invisible at the call site. The abstraction actively encourages writing code that would be fine for an in-memory list and is an N+1 query disaster against a real database.
The per-aggregate split has to be designed up front; without discipline the mechanical one-repository-per-table mapping returns, and aggregate boundaries are lost in the process.

Transaction control does not belong here: a repository that flushes or commits per call turns one business operation into several partial commits, so the unit of work must be understood and kept outside.
In languages without a framework surface (C, C++, Go, Rust) the whole structure — interface, implementation, row-to-object mapping, test double — is maintained by hand.
Repositories drift with query needs: as reporting requirements change, method counts grow and review cost rises unless criteria are factored into Query Objects or Specifications.

The pattern fights CQRS-style read paths: forcing reporting queries through an aggregate-oriented repository interface produces either method explosion or over-fetching whole aggregates just to read a couple of fields.

participants.responsibility: Collection-like interface for one aggregate: add, remove, find by identity, and domain-language query methods; hides query construction, the mapping layer and the store.
Constructs query specifications declaratively and submits them to the repository; works with collections of domain objects and never sees queries or persistence APIs.
Persistence-ignorant objects that carry behaviour and invariants; the only things the repository returns and accepts.
Converts domain objects to rows and back; the repository delegates all loading and storing to it and adds no mapping logic of its own.
Tracks changed objects, provides the identity map and performs flush/commit; the repository never commits on its own.
Reusable declarative criteria submitted to the repository, keeping composable query logic out of both callers and the repository interface.

use_cases: DDD application services that must load an aggregate root, run domain logic on it and store it again without knowing the table layout.
Data-mapper backends where several application services and background jobs share recurring complex queries (overdue invoices, pending orders, open tickets).
Applications that must be unit-testable away from the database: repositories are the substitution point for in-memory doubles.
Systems that must support more than one store behind a stable domain interface — relational in production, in-memory in tests, a document store for a particular deployment.
Uniform cross-cutting access policy for an aggregate: caching, read-replica routing, audit logging or authorization applied as decorators around one interface.
Migration work where the persistence technology changes (ORM swap, schema split, service extraction) while the domain model and its tests stay untouched.
CQRS write-side aggregate loading where the aggregate must be reconstructed fully to apply business rules and enforce invariants.
Integration with heterogeneous data sources where one repository unifies access to a cache, primary database and a third-party API behind a domain interface.

Spring Data JPA applications can use Repository/CrudRepository for aggregate-typed CRUD, paging and derived queries, then add only domain-specific methods rather than wrapping every persistence operation.
The .NET eShopOnContainers ordering microservice uses an EF Core BuyerRepository over a shared scoped DbContext/unit of work, while CQRS/Dapper handles presentation reads.
Python applications using SQLAlchemy ORM can place an aggregate-facing repository over Session, whose identity map and unit-of-work flush semantics provide the mapper/session boundary.
avoid_when: Straight CRUD over one table with little domain logic: an Active Record model, a Table Data Gateway, or DbSet/Repository<T> used directly is simpler.
Ad-hoc reporting and analytics: query builders, hand-written SQL in a read model, or a CQRS read side are clearer and faster than bending a collection interface to aggregate functions.
The persistence framework already supplies the repository surface and the store will never be swapped: a one-to-one wrapper duplicates the API, hides features and adds indirection.
Transactions must span several aggregates or stores: put the boundary in the unit of work or application service, not in a repository.
The system is a transaction script with a thin data carrier model: the extra layer costs maintenance without buying domain separation.
The query language is the domain (search engines, graph traversals): express it in a Query Object or a dedicated query service instead of forcing it into finder methods.
Anemic domain model where entities are pure data carriers: a repository on top of an anemic model is just a DAO with extra steps — Active Record or direct ORM usage is cleaner.
The team cannot articulate a second concrete implementation of the interface: abstraction without optionality is just indirection.
anti_patterns: Repository per table: a mechanical one-to-one mapping of tables to repositories with generic CRUD, which hides the relational structure and destroys aggregate boundaries.
Generic repository exposing IQueryable, query builders or expression trees, so callers still write the queries — the pattern's purpose inverted, with an extra layer on top.
Repository that only wraps an ORM one-to-one (one method per ORM method, ORM entities in the signature): nothing is encapsulated and the ORM's features are hidden for no benefit.
Repository that commits or opens its own transaction per call, turning one business operation into several partial commits and silently breaking the unit of work.
Repository returning DTOs, serialized rows or persistence records instead of domain objects — the layer has degenerated into a data access object.
In-memory test repositories that do not reproduce the real query semantics (ordering, uniqueness, null handling), so production defects pass the suite.
Multiple repositories each committing independently without a coordinating Unit of Work: one operation can partially succeed, leaving the system in an inconsistent state under load.

Cargo-cult Repository: applying the pattern because 'repositories are best practice' when the domain is anemic or the store will never be swapped — abstraction without a second implementation is just indirection.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: domain decisions are separated from persistence mechanics and query construction.
Dependency inversion: the domain defines the collection interface, infrastructure implements it for a concrete store.
Information hiding / encapsulation: SQL, table and column names, sessions and mapping stay behind the interface.
Persistence ignorance of the domain model: the repository is the domain's own vocabulary for storing and retrieving its objects.
Single responsibility: one repository per aggregate root, one reason to change (the persistence of that aggregate).
Interface segregation: expose only the queries the domain needs, not the whole mapper or ORM surface.

Command-Query Separation (CQRS): queries (read, no state change) and commands (write, state change) may use different paths; forcing reads through an aggregate-write repository interface is often a mismatch for reporting use cases.
Liskov Substitution: any implementation of a repository interface — in-memory fake, test double, different storage backend — must be substitutable without callers detecting the difference.
best_practices: Define one repository per aggregate root, never one per table, and enforce the rule with a marker interface or generic constraint where the language allows it.
Declare the repository interface in the domain layer and implement it in infrastructure; inject the implementation so the domain never names a store.
Return domain objects and collections from the interface; keep query builders, expression trees, tracked entities and row types inside the implementation.
Leave flush and commit to the unit of work or application service; repository methods only add, remove, find and query — never manage transaction boundaries.
Name methods in domain language (findOverdueInvoices, findActiveOrdersForUser) and factor reusable criteria into Query Objects or Specifications instead of stacking finder methods.
Attach caching, logging, audit and authorization as decorators around the interface rather than repeating them in every repository.

Provide in-memory implementations for tests, and verify the semantics they fake (filtering, ordering, uniqueness, transactional visibility) — a fake that returns unsorted results on every call hides real bugs.
Review the SQL the collection calls actually emit (query logging, generated SQL) so hidden round trips and N+1 loads surface before production.

Python / SQLAlchemy 2.0: use Mapped[...] + mapped_column() for type-safe declarations; migrate from session.query() to the unified select() API with session.scalars(); attach loader strategies (selectinload, joinedload) at query time to structurally prevent N+1.

Python / SQLAlchemy 2.0: never place commit() in repository methods — the transaction boundary (how far one unit of work extends) belongs to the use-case or application service layer that coordinates across repositories.

Python / AsyncSession: avoid implicit IO by enforcing eager loading; set expire_on_commit=False to keep objects usable after a flush; use raiseload as a guard to catch lazy-loading-at-production-time early.

Generic repository base classes are acceptable for reducing CRUD boilerplate but must be constrained to aggregate-root types and must not expose IQueryable or raw query-builder objects across the interface.

Prefer purpose-built query methods (findByEmail, findOverdue) over a single generic method accepting a predicate; the former makes query intent explicit and reviewable by domain experts, the latter scatters query logic into callers.

Integration-test repository implementations against a real database (or test container) rather than relying solely on mocked repositories in unit tests — mocking hides interaction bugs between the app and the actual persistence layer.

https://martinfowler.com/eaaCatalog/repository.html — Canonical online description by Hieatt and Mee.

https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/20/orm/queryguide/query-guide.html — SQLAlchemy 2.0 unified select() API, loader strategies (selectinload, joinedload, raiseload), identity map, and session lifecycle.

Tomoda Hinata, 'SQLAlchemy 2.0 Practical Guide: Designing a Type-Safe ORM Data-Access Layer That Survives Production' (2026) — production Python/SQLAlchemy 2.0 layered architecture: Router → UseCase → Repository → Model; N+1 structural prevention with selectinload; transaction boundary discipline.
https://calmops.com/software-engineering/database-design-patterns/ — Repository vs Unit of Work vs Data Mapper vs Active Record comparison, with transaction consistency guidance.

https://bigmachine.io/articles/databases/repositories-on-top-unitofwork-are-not-a-good-idea — Critical analysis: Repository wrapping an ORM's Unit of Work (EF DbContext) is an abstraction over an abstraction; repositories and Unit of Work don't mix when each repository independently commits.

https://bubble.ro/2026/07/08/the-repository-pattern-useful-abstraction-or-cargo-cult/ — Honest assessment: Repository earns its cost only with real aggregates and invariants; generic IQueryable repositories, cargo-cult application, and N+1 traps; CQRS complementarity.
https://www.baeldung.com/java-dao-vs-repository — DAO vs Repository distinction: DAO is table-centric and lower-level; Repository is domain-centric and aggregates DAOs for complex domain operations.

https://remki.hashnode.dev/enterprise-design-patterns-implementing-the-repository-pattern-with-python-and-sqlalchemy — Enterprise Python/SQLAlchemy Repository implementation with Data Mapper, Identity Map, and Unit of Work coordination.
